fullText:
Summary: CIC Holdings (CIC.N0000 voting, CIC.X0000 non-voting) is a solid, growing group, but the voting shares are priced above what the numbers support. At Rs 27.80 the voting share trades at 1.09x its group NAV of Rs 25.52 and 7.1x trailing earnings, with only a 1.8% dividend yield because the company pays out about 14% of profit. Returns on equity of 15–16% are below the 18% return I require, so the methods put fair value at about Rs 22.60, and the voting share is about 23% above it. The non-voting share, with the same dividends and earnings, trades at Rs 23.90 (14% cheaper), about 6% above fair value, so it's the better way in. I'd buy at up to about Rs 19.20 and treat under Rs 17 as a strong buy. About two-thirds of NAV is CIC's stake in John Keells, carried at book value.

Price and key figures
Price: voting Rs 27.80 and non-voting Rs 23.90 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-06). Please check them live. In April–September 2026 the voting share traded between Rs 27.00 and Rs 32.00, and it closed the year to March 2026 at Rs 29.90. All per-share figures are after the 1-for-5 share split of October 2025.
Six months to 30 September 2026 (group, unaudited): revenue rose 3% to Rs 42.9bn and profit attributable to shareholders rose 22% to Rs 3.17bn. EPS was Rs 1.67 against Rs 1.37.
What drove it: livestock solutions (results up 31%), industrial solutions (up 47%) and health and personal care (up 10%) grew, while agri solutions fell (revenue down 12%, results down 27%). The share of associates' profit, mainly John Keells, rose to Rs 673mn from Rs 275mn. Net finance costs rose 26% to Rs 1.33bn.
Year to March 2026 (group): revenue Rs 91.8bn (up 10%), profit attributable Rs 6.91bn (up 27%), EPS Rs 3.64 (Rs 2.87), ROE 15%, NAV Rs 24.37, dividend Rs 0.50 (14% of profit). Debt Rs 30.2bn, 56% of equity.
John Keells: CIC equity-accounts its effective holding of about 6% of John Keells Holdings. Its share of JKH's net assets was Rs 33.4bn at 30 June 2026, about Rs 17.60 of CIC's Rs 25.52 NAV per share. It's carried at book value, not JKH's market price.

Methods
NAV (Rs 25.52): voting 1.09x, non-voting 0.94x. The voting share fails your NAV rule if it's above 1.0x; the non-voting share passes.
Return on equity: 15% for the year to March 2026 and about 16.5% over the last 12 months; 14% in the year to March 2025.
P/E: 7.1x trailing EPS of Rs 3.94 (voting). Year-end P/E (voting): 8.2x (2026), 8.2x (2025), 2.7x (2024), 3.5x (2023), 3.9x (2022).
Dividends: Rs 0.50 a year, a 1.8% yield, about 14% of profit.
Debt: Rs 30.2bn at March 2026, 56% of equity; net finance costs up 26% in the half.
Justified price to book: Rs 13.6 / 19.1 / 26.9 across the cases, weighted Rs 19.0.
P/E method: Rs 21.6 / 33.6 / 45.0, weighted Rs 32.3.
Residual income: Rs 9.0 / 16.8 / 27.7, weighted Rs 16.6.
Dividend model: Rs 3.3 / 4.9 / 8.0 (not used in the fair value).

CIC keeps about 86% of its profit, so a dividend model badly understates it and I've left it out of the average. A cash-flow DCF also doesn't suit it right now: it is investing heavily (investing outflows of Rs 5.5bn in the year to March 2025) and much of its profit is its share of John Keells, which isn't paid in cash. The book-value methods are lower than the P/E method because ROE of 15–16% is below the 18% required return.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 20% / 18% / 16.5%.
Long-run ROE (price to book): 13% / 15% / 17%.
ROE path (residual income): 15% falling to 12% / 16% falling to 15% / 17% held.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 3.6 × 6 / 4.2 × 8 / 4.5 × 10.
Average of the three methods: Rs 14.7 / Rs 23.2 / Rs 33.2.
Common: Sri Lankan 7–10-year government bonds yield about 12% (October 2026), plus a premium for a diversified group with rising debt. In the base case, the second half grows about 10% on last year's, giving EPS of about Rs 4.20 for the year to March 2027.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 22.60 (0.89x NAV). The voting share at Rs 27.80 is about 23% above it; the non-voting share at Rs 23.90 is about 6% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 19.20, and 25% gives Rs 17.00. The same levels apply to the non-voting share, since it has the same economic rights.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 22.50, 150 at up to Rs 19.20 and 150 at up to Rs 17.00. That averages about Rs 19.86, about Rs 9,930, against Rs 13,900 for voting shares at Rs 27.80.
Realism: the voting share's low in April–September 2026 was Rs 27.00, so Rs 22.50 needs about a 19% fall in it. The non-voting share (Rs 23.90) needs only about a 6% fall to reach the first tier, so watch it. Rs 19.20 needs a broader fall.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 16%: 14.8 / 22.6 / 32.0 for long-run ROE of 12% / 15% / 18%.
Cost of equity 18%: 11.3 / 16.8 / 23.5.
Cost of equity 20%: 8.9 / 13.0 / 18.0.
On book value, today's voting price needs a 16% cost of equity and a long-run ROE of about 17%.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: agri solutions recovering; livestock, industrial and health growth continuing; John Keells' profits rising (CIC's share is now a big part of earnings); a higher dividend payout; lower interest rates, which would cut finance costs and the cost of equity.
Supports a lower value: rising debt and finance costs; weather, fertiliser prices or policy changes hurting agri solutions; John Keells' share price staying below the book value CIC carries it at; a weaker rupee raising imported raw material costs; the controlling shareholder's interests differing from minority shareholders'.

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 and the interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
